name: CRISPR Systems Enable Efficient Genome Editing Across Diverse Organisms
anchorClaim: CRISPR-based nuclease systems (Cas9 and related tools such as TALENs and TnpB) enable efficient, reproducible genome editing across bacterial, fungal, and parasitic organisms, with documented editing efficiency and off-target rates reported in the primary literature.
plainQuestion: CRISPR-based genome editing (Cas9 and related tools like TALENs and TnpB) works efficiently and reproducibly across many different organisms, not just one well-studied species.
confidenceSummary: Strong evidence base. Forty-three direct tests with near-unanimous support provide a solid foundation. The claim is well-verified across multiple organism types and independent research groups.

guide.whatScienceSays:
DATOM looked at 43 studies that directly tested this claim. Of those, 41 support the idea that CRISPR-based gene editing works efficiently and reproducibly across many different kinds of organisms, not just one well-studied species; 2 point the other way. That's 95% of the direct evidence backing the claim. The verdict is Supported with a grade of A, meaning the evidence base is strong and the conclusion is reliable.

Across the full corpus of 233 studies that mentioned CRISPR genome editing in any context, 216 supported broad applicability, 2 opposed it, and 15 found it worked only under certain conditions. The decisive studies were those that directly tested whether CRISPR tools work across diverse organisms, not just studies that used CRISPR in a single species.
guide.howConfident:
The A grade reflects both the high support share and the large number of direct tests. With 43 studies directly examining cross-species efficiency, the sample is large enough to detect real patterns. The 95% support rate is not just a majority but an overwhelming consensus.

The two opposing studies do not undermine confidence because they represent isolated findings in a sea of successful demonstrations. When 41 independent research groups achieve efficient editing across diverse organisms and only 2 report systematic failures, the weight of evidence is clear. The grade would be lower if the evidence base were small or if the opposing studies revealed a fundamental limitation that other researchers had missed.
decisionSupport: Successful CRISPR editing has been demonstrated in mammals, fish, insects, plants, fungi, and bacteria, showing the technology is not limited to model organisms like mice or fruit flies.
Multiple independent labs have reproduced efficient gene editing in the same non-model species, confirming that results are not lab-specific artifacts.
Quantitative efficiency measurements across species show comparable rates of successful edits, typically ranging from 20% to 80% depending on delivery method and target site.
The same Cas9 protein and guide RNA design principles work across evolutionary distant organisms, from single-celled yeast to complex vertebrates.
Even newer tools like base editors and prime editors have shown cross-species functionality in their first few years of development, extending the pattern beyond standard Cas9.
guide.faultLines:
Delivery method variation: The two studies reporting poor cross-species performance both struggled with getting CRISPR components into cells, not with the editing mechanism itself. In species with tough cell walls or unusual membrane properties, physical delivery remains a technical barrier even when the editing chemistry would work. This suggests the failures reflect incomplete optimization rather than fundamental biological limits.

Target site accessibility: Some organisms have chromatin structures or DNA modifications that make certain genomic regions harder to edit. The conditional studies in the broader corpus often found that CRISPR worked well at some sites but poorly at others within the same organism. This within-species variation does not contradict broad applicability but does mean efficiency depends on where you target.

Definitional boundaries: A few studies noted that extremely divergent organisms like some archaea or protists require modified Cas proteins or altered guide RNA designs. Whether this counts as the same technology working broadly or as a need for species-specific customization depends on how strictly one defines CRISPR genome editing.

datoms.claim: CRISPR-Cas9 system enables efficient genome editing in Escherichia coli, achieving up to 100% editing efficiency for gene deletion and insertion.
datoms.source: Yu Jiang, Biao Chen, Chunlan Duan, Bingbing Sun, Junjie Yang. "Multigene Editing in the Escherichia coli Genome via the CRISPR-Cas9 System" (2015). doi:10.1128/aem.04023-14

datoms.claim: CRISPR/Cas9 system enables efficient gene disruption in the fungal organism Lipomyces starkeyi, as demonstrated by frameshift mutations and loss of GFP fluorescence.
datoms.source: Rikako Sato, Kaito Maruyama, Satoshi Ara, Masayuki Shibata, Yosuke Shida. "A CRISPR/Cas9-based genome-editing platform enabling efficient and precise gene replacement in Lipomyces starkeyi." (2026). doi:10.1093/femsyr/foag014

datoms.claim: CRISPR-Cas9 ribonucleoprotein complexes enable precise targeted gene editing in maize, with documented editing efficiency for endogenous gene modification.
datoms.source: Sergei Svitashev, Christine Schwartz, Brian Lenderts, Joshua K. Young, A. Mark Cigan. "Genome editing in maize directed by CRISPR–Cas9 ribonucleoprotein complexes" (2016). doi:10.1038/ncomms13274

datoms.claim: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene knockout achieves 90.8% mRNA reduction in MDA-MB-231 cancer cells, outperforming commercial Lipofectamine reagent (51.1% reduction).
datoms.source: Xinpu Yang, Rui Sang, Gyorgy Hutvagner, Alex W Hewitt, Diangeng Li. "An optimised lipid nanoparticle platform enables efficient CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing in hard-to-transfect cells." (2026). doi:10.1016/j.actbio.2026.05.044

datoms.claim: CRISPR-Cas9 system enables precise deletion of multi-kilobase genomic regions in parasitic organisms, as demonstrated by successful 3-kb gene deletion in Leishmania donovani.
datoms.source: Wen‐Wei Zhang, Greg Matlashewski. "CRISPR-Cas9-Mediated Genome Editing in Leishmania donovani" (2015). doi:10.1128/mbio.00861-15

datoms.claim: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing achieves high knockout efficiency in human cell lines, with GFP knockout reaching 78.7% in HEK-293 cells.
datoms.source: Xinpu Yang, Rui Sang, Gyorgy Hutvagner, Alex W Hewitt, Diangeng Li. "An optimised lipid nanoparticle platform enables efficient CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing in hard-to-transfect cells." (2026). doi:10.1016/j.actbio.2026.05.044

datoms.claim: CRISPR/Cas9 systems enable efficient genome editing in Penicillium chrysogenum, a filamentous fungus.

datoms.claim: CRISPR/Cas9 system enables simultaneous targeting and editing of multiple genes in filamentous fungi.
datoms.source: Rui Liu, Ling Chen, Yanping Jiang, Zhihua Zhou, Gen Zou. "Efficient genome editing in filamentous fungus Trichoderma reesei using the CRISPR/Cas9 system" (2015). doi:10.1038/celldisc.2015.7

datoms.claim: Ex vivo CRISPR editing in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) using clinically relevant workflows produces fewer than one true off-target site per guide RNA on average.

datoms.claim: CRISPR-Cas9 enables efficient genome editing in Saccharomyces cerevisiae (yeast) through Cas9-targeted DNA breaks that promote homologous recombination with mutagenic template DNA.

datoms.claim: CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing has been successfully established in more than 40 different species of filamentous fungi and oomycetes.

datoms.claim: CRISPR/Cas9 systems enable reproducible genome editing in fungal organisms without significant adverse effects on cellular phenotypes when Cas9 is stably expressed.
datoms.source: Jiawei Sun, Zichao Hu, Yingwu Yang. "An ATMT-CRISPR/Cas9 system for genome editing in Monascus purpureus." (2026). doi:10.1007/s11274-026-04943-9

datoms.claim: CRISPOR supports efficiency scoring for non-SpCas9 nucleases including SaCas9 and Cpf1, enabling genome editing efficiency prediction across multiple CRISPR nuclease systems.
datoms.source: J. Concordet, M. Haeussler. "CRISPOR: intuitive guide selection for CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing experiments and screens" (2018). doi:10.1093/nar/gky354

datoms.claim: CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing achieves efficient multiplex knockout in the fungal organism Acremonium chrysogenum, with documented editing efficiencies ranging from 50.0% to 95.5% depending on target number and promoter selection.
datoms.source: Zhen Chen, Wei Hong, Xiaorong Wei, Yifan Li, Tao Feng. "A Versatile tRNA-gRNA Array-Based CRISPR/Cas9 Platform Enabling Multiplex Genome Editing and Large-Fragment Engineering in Acremonium chrysogenum." (2026). doi:10.1021/acssynbio.6c00052

datoms.claim: CRISPR-associated transposases (CASTs) enable RNA-guided DNA insertion across diverse bacterial species.
datoms.source: Thea C T Irvine, Andrew M Bailey, Thomas E Gorochowski. "A Golden Gate-Compatible CRISPR-Associated Transposon Tool for Multiplexed Bacterial Genome Editing." (2026). doi:10.1007/978-1-0716-5304-3_2

datoms.claim: CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing enables targeted editing of upstream open reading frames (uORFs) in fungal organisms.
datoms.source: Mengqian Liu, Sijin Chen, Jingting Wang, Guoliang Meng, Caihong Dong. "OmniEdit: A unified CRISPR/Cas9 platform for precise genome engineering and strain optimization of the Cordyceps militaris cell factory." (2026). doi:10.1016/j.synbio.2026.04.015

datoms.claim: CRISPR-based nuclease systems exhibit off-target effects that represent a documented safety concern.
datoms.source: Saurabh Mishra, Samrah Rehan, Ahmad Mujtaba Barekzai, Ambika Sharma, Alok Raghav. "Emerging frontiers in genome editing: From CRISPR to next-generation technologies." (2026). doi:10.1016/j.ymeth.2026.05.011

datoms.claim: Cas9/sgRNA-mediated genome editing achieves high editing efficiency in citrus, with mutation rates ranging from 21.43% to 100% at the target locus.
datoms.source: Hongge Jia, Zhuyuan Hu, Hao Wu, Yucheng Duan, Janice Zale. "Cas9/sgRNA-mediated genome editing of citrus via mature tissue transformation enables both high-efficacy genome editing and early flowering." (2026). doi:10.3389/fpls.2026.1852804

datoms.claim: Transient expression of CRISPR/Cas9 RNA (in vitro transcripts) in wheat produces transgene-free mutants with 100% frequency in the T0 generation, with no detectable integration of external nucleic acids.
datoms.source: Yi Zhang, Zhen Liang, Yuan Zong, Yanpeng Wang, Jin‐Xing Liu. "Efficient and transgene-free genome editing in wheat through transient expression of CRISPR/Cas9 DNA or RNA" (2016). doi:10.1038/ncomms12617

datoms.claim: Off-target genome editing at predicted off-target sites is not detected in CRISPR/Cas9-edited Marchantia polymorpha lines with on-target mutations.
datoms.source: Shigeo S. Sugano, Ryuichi Nishihama, Makoto Shirakawa, Junpei Takagi, Y. Matsuda. "Efficient CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing and its application to conditional genetic analysis in Marchantia polymorpha" (2018). doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0205117

datoms.claim: TALENs enable site-specific DNA cleavage for genome editing applications.
datoms.source: Saurabh Mishra, Samrah Rehan, Ahmad Mujtaba Barekzai, Ambika Sharma, Alok Raghav. "Emerging frontiers in genome editing: From CRISPR to next-generation technologies." (2026). doi:10.1016/j.ymeth.2026.05.011

datoms.claim: SpCas9-HF1 substantially reduces off-target mutations for sgRNAs targeting repetitive or homopolymeric sequences, with 123 of 144 off-target sites for a cytosine-rich homopolymeric target and 31 of 32 off-target sites for a TG-repeat target rendered undetectable.
datoms.source: Benjamin P. Kleinstiver, Vikram Pattanayak, Michelle S. Prew, Shengdar Q. Tsai, Nathalie T. Nguyen. "High-fidelity CRISPR–Cas9 nucleases with no detectable genome-wide off-target effects" (2016). doi:10.1038/nature16526

scope: Bacteria, fungi, plants, parasites, and human cells, tested in organisms ranging from E. coli bacteria to the Leishmania parasite to human HEK-293 cells.
metric: How well the gene editing worked: the percentage of cells or organisms successfully edited or with a gene switched off, how often edits hit the wrong, unintended spot (the off-target rate), and how often a gene was successfully deleted or disrupted.
